metadata.title: Dr.avx Artifact Evaluation Guide
metadata.description:
Dr.avx Artifact Evaluation Guide

1. Pre-Requistes

 To ensure the successful evaluation of this artifact, please provision an environment that meets the following hardware and software requirements.

  • Hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6342 (Ice Lake) server
        - Other AVX-512-enabled Intel Server CPUs (Xeon) are also available. Use lscpu | grep avx512 on the Xeon server to validate AVX-512 capability. (e.g.,  Xeon series: Cascade Lake, Ice Lake)
  • Cores: Available CPU cores >= 24. 
      - For optimal performance, it is highly recommended to use as many cores as possible, preferably located on the same NUMA node (Socket).
  • Docker version: 28.1.1
      - While other Docker versions or compatible CRI runtimes (e.g., Podman) may function, they have not been tested for compatibility with this artifact.
  • Disk Space: >= 500 GB
      - Database-related workloads generate significant log data during evaluation, requiring ample storage.
  • Compilation Requirements: None.
       - The artifact is fully containerized. All required binaries and libraries have been pre-built and are included in the Docker image. No local compilation is necessary.
  • Binary: The Dockerhub Docker image base: dravx-ae/latest
  • Download Time: 15~30 minutes from Zenodo, up to your network.
  • Estimated Experiment Time: 3 hours.
  • Key Results to be Reproduced:  Figure 10a, Figure 10b, Figure 11

2. Quick Start

Step 1: Download the Docker Image 

Click and download the pre-configured compressed artifact image from Zenodo. You will receive a file named `dravx_ae.tar.gz`.

Step 2: Uncompress Docker Image

Use gzip to manually uncompress the image file. This will yield a file named dravx_ae.tar. The process takes approximately 2 minutes.

gzip -d dravx_ae.tar.gz 

Step 3: Import Docker Image

Import the Docker image, and use `docker image ls` to validate.

docker import - dravx_ae < dravx_ae.tar

Step 4: Run the Instruction Rewriting Examples 

This command runs the 5 instructions illustrated in paper Fig. 7. Dr.avx will print the detailed rewritten instruction sequence in the output.

docker run --rm dravx_ae:latest /eval/run.sh --fig7

Example output (part of Fig. 7d):

[REWRITE INFO]: ====   Rewriting vprorq    ====
vprorq {%k0} $0x01 %ymm2 -> %ymm3
  mask: %k0
  src1: $0x01
  src2: %ymm2
  dst: %ymm3
[DEBUG]: ==== INSTRUCTION SEQUENCE ====
vmovdqu %ymm10 -> %gs:0x00000300[32byte]
vmovdqu %ymm11 -> %gs:0x00000340[32byte]
vmovdqu %ymm2 -> %ymm10
vmovdqu %ymm2 -> %ymm11
vpsllq $0x3f %ymm10 -> %ymm10
vpsrlq $0x01 %ymm11 -> %ymm11
vpor   %ymm11 %ymm10 -> %ymm3
vmovdqu %gs:0x00000300[32byte] -> %ymm10
vmovdqu %gs:0x00000340[32byte] -> %ymm11
[DEBUG]: ==============================

 

Step 5: Run the Full Evaluation (Approx. 3 Hours)

This command runs the complete, scaled-down evaluation pipeline. It will create two directories in your current working path ($(pwd)):

  * figs/: Contains the generated performance plots (PDF/PNG).
  * results/: Contains the raw performance logs from all experiments.

# Ensure you have at least 24 physical cores available (e.g., 0-23)
# Use sudo if your user is not in the 'docker' group
docker run --cpuset-cpus="0-23" \
  -v $(pwd)/figs:/eval/figs \
  dravx_ae:latest \
  /eval/run.sh --all

Noted: We highly recommend running the experiments on a dedicated machine with no other workloads to minimize interference and ensure stable, reproducible results for performance-sensitive benchmarks (especially databases and LLM inference).

Step 6: View Results

Upon successful completion, the figs directory will be populated with the result plots.

```bash
./figs
├── Fig10.a_mysql.pdf
├── Fig10.a_mysql.png
├── Fig10.b_mongodb.pdf
├── Fig10.b_mongodb.png
├── Fig11.pdf
└── Fig11.png
```

3. Advanced Usage

Instead of running the full suite, you can execute individual experiments or inspect the available options.

Display Help

To view all available parameters and experiment flags, use the `-h` or `--help` argument.

docker run --rm dravx_ae:latest /eval/run.sh -h

Run Individual Experiments

The commands below demonstrate the configurations used in the artifact evaluation. These are scaled-down versions (fewer repetitions, smaller datasets) to ensure a reasonable execution time. In contrast, the **full-scale configurations** used in our paper involved *20* repetitions for Llama,  *1800s* per scenario for MySQL, and a *36,000,000*-record scale for MongoDB.

Llama Workload (Fig. 11)

docker run --rm --cpuset-cpus="0-8" \
  -v $(pwd)/figs:/eval/figs \
  dravx_ae:latest /eval/run.sh \
  --llama --llama-reps 3

MySQL Workload (Fig. 10a)


docker run --rm --cpuset-cpus="0-23" \
  -v $(pwd)/figs:/eval/figs \
  dravx_ae:latest /eval/run.sh \
  --mysql \
  --mysql-threads 16 --mysql-time 180

MongoDB Workload (Fig. 10b)


docker run --rm --cpuset-cpus="0-23" \
  -v $(pwd)/figs:/eval/figs \
  dravx_ae:latest /eval/run.sh \
  --mongodb \
  --mongodb-threads 16 --mongodb-count 7200000

4. Evaluation and Expected Output

Expected Output Files

The primary output consists of the PDF and PNG plots corresponding to the figures in the paper's evaluation section (Fig. 10a, Fig10b, Fig. 11).

⚠️ Note on Performance Variability

It is expected that the absolute performance numbers (e.g., raw throughput, latency) generated by this artifact differ from those reported in the paper. Performance fluctuations are normal and can be attributed to several factors:

  • Scaled-Down Configuration: The default AE scripts use reduced iterations, smaller datasets, and shorter run times (approx. 3 hours) compared to the full-scale experiments (approx. 2 days).
  • Hardware Differences: Variations in the host machine's specific CPU frequency, cache sizes, memory, and NUMA topology will impact results.
  • System and Containerization Overhead: Factors such as host OS background processes and Docker's scheduling and resource management can introduce non-negligible performance variations, sometimes even affect the whole evaluation.

The primary goal of this artifact is to reproduce the relative performance trends and speedups presented in the paper. These relative trends should remain consistent despite variations in the absolute performance values.

metadata.title: Artifact for "Revealing the Dark Side of Smart Accounts: An Empirical Study of EIP-7702 Incurred Risks in Blockchain Ecosystem"
metadata.description:
# EIP-7702 Malicious Contract Detection Tool

This repository contains the source code and intermediate results for detecting malicious smart contracts targeting EIP-7702 smart accounts.  
The detection framework contains three pipelines for corresponding attack categories**:

1. **EOA-targeted attacks** – malicious contracts aiming at externally owned accounts.
2. **CA-targeted attacks** – malicious contracts aiming at vulnerable smart contracts.
3. **Composite attacks** – combined scenarios aiming at both EOAs and CAs.


---

## 📂 Repository Structure

| File / Folder | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `get_code/` | Scripts to fetch contract bytecode from blockchain explorers (e.g., Etherscan API). This is the first stage of all three detection pipelines. |
| `decompile/` | Main detection entry point. Loads decompiled results and applies detection rules for EOA-targeted, CA-targeted, or composite attacks. |
| `decompile/crosscontract_sh/` | Scripts for cross-contract analysis, enabling the detection of multi-contract attack patterns. |
| `contracts_with_bytecode.xlsx` | Intermediate dataset containing all addresses with successfully retrieved bytecode. Can be used to skip the `get_code/` step. |
| `output_#.zip` | Archived intermediate dataset for #-targeted detection. Contains detected malicious contract reports and logs. Can be used to skip the `get_code/` step. |
| `AM_Detect_FlashloanCall.jsonl` | Intermediate detection output for suspicious flash loan calls observed in EOA-targeted or composite attacks. Can be used to skip the `decompile/` step. |
| `AM_FunctionSelector.jsonl` | Intermediate detection output for mapping between function selectors and their decompiled semantics, used for identifying malicious function patterns. Can be used to skip the `decompile/` step. |
| `result.jsonl result.xlsx` | Detection result. |
| `analysis_information/` | Finding related dataset, including obfuscated vulnerable contract code example and malicious smart account addresses. |

---

## Reproduction Guide

The pipeline supports **restarting from any intermediate stage** using the saved files we mentioned before.

### **Full Pipeline**
```bash
# Example: ca_detect

# Step 1: Retrieve bytecode, you may need to change file path, and use a valid API key
python ./ca_detect/main.py
python ./ca_detect/get_code.py


# Step 2: Decompile with Gigahorse, https://github.com/nevillegrech/gigahorse-toolchain#

mv ca_detect/decompile/main.py ./gigahorse
mv ca_detect/decompile/env.yaml ./gigahorse
mv ca_detect/decompile/run_analysis.sh ./gigahorse
mv ca_detect/decompile/analyze.dl ./gigahorse/clients


# Step 3: Run main detection
python ./gigahorse/main.py

mv ca_detect/decompile/AM_Detect_FlashloanCall.jsonl ./ca_detect/decompile/crosscontract_sh
mv ca_detect/decompile/AM_FunctionSelector.jsonl ./ca_detect/decompile/crosscontract_sh
python ./ca_detect/decompile/crosscontract_sh/cross_match.py
```

---

### **2. Starting from Bytecode or Decompiled Results**
```bash
# Starting from Bytecode

mv ca_detect/decompile/main.py ./gigahorse
mv ca_detect/decompile/env.yaml ./gigahorse
mv ca_detect/decompile/run_analysis.sh ./gigahorse
mv ca_detect/decompile/analyze.dl ./gigahorse/clients
python ./gigahorse/main.py


# Starting from Decompiled Results

python ./ca_detect/decompile/crosscontract_sh/cross_match.py
```


---

## Dependencies

- **Python3** 
- **Gigahorse Decompiler** (Source Code Deployment)
- **API access to blockchain explorers** (Etherscan, Infura)  


---

## Notes
- **Intermediate files** are intentionally preserved to allow partial pipeline execution without re-fetching or re-decompiling contracts.
- The cross-contract analysis stage is critical for detecting ca and composite attacks involving multiple interacting contracts. 
- If the python file do not works, check the path and .env file, making sure all APIs and file paths are correct. 

## Ethics Statement
This research is conducted solely for academic and security purposes.
All detection tools, experiments, and released datasets are designed only to identify attacker-controlled smart contracts associated with EIP-7702 malicious activities.

**No victim identification** – This dataset does not and cannot reveal the identities of victim addresses, ensuring that no sensitive or private user data is exposed.

metadata.title: FlippyRAM
metadata.description:
Note: This is an archived version used for artifact evaluation. Refer to https://github.com/iisys-sns/FlippyRAM/ for future updates.

 

We developed a new framework to check if your system is vulnerable to Rowhammer, incorporating the state-of-the-art Rowhammer techniques and tools. Thus, we invite everyone to participate in this unique opportunity to join forces and close this research gap together. We address the following questions:

  • What is the real-world prevalence of the Rowhammer effect?
  • How many systems, in their current configurations, are vulnerable to Rowhammer?

As large-scale studies with hundreds to thousands of systems are not easy to perform, such a study has not yet been performed.

metadata.title: Towards Threading the Needle of Debuggable Optimized Binaries
metadata.description:
This is the artifact for the paper ``Towards Threading the Needle of Debuggable Optimized Binaries'', to appear in Proceedings of CGO 26.

It contains the source code of DebugTuner, a framework for measuring the impact of single optimizing transformations on software debuggability and guiding the construction of debug-friendly optimization levels with low performance overhead.

The source code is also available at: https://github.com/Sap4Sec/debugtuner

hits.title: Towards Threading the Needle of Debuggable Optimized Binaries

metadata.title: Vlasiator
metadata.description:
This new Vlasiator release adds:

  • Full support for GPU computation on HPC environments to Vlasiator, targeting both Nvidia (CUDA) and AMD (HIP) platforms.
  • A subgrid-scale wave-particle scattering model (implemented as velocity space diffusion) has been added for magnetosheath waves.
  • Vorticity and temperature / pressure anisotropy can now be taken into account for mesh refinement criteria.
  • Improved the code's runtime resilience by including a mechanism to write frequent recovery files using a circular buffer scheme.
  • The code is now ported (or portable) to all EuroHPC machines, as of December 2025.
  • In addition, there are a large number of bugfixes to time-varying inflow, system boundary handling, ionosphere stability and overall quality of life.

More detailed list of what's Changed:

metadata.title: Automatic Data Enumeration for Fast Collections
metadata.description:
Artifact for "Automatic Data Enumeration for Fast Collections", accepted at CGO'26

 

Abstract:

Data collections provide a powerful abstraction to organize data, simplifying development and maintenance. Choosing an implementation for each collection is a critical decision, with performance, memory and energy tradeoffs that need to be balanced for each use case. Specialized implementations offer significant benefits over their general-purpose counterparts, but also require certain properties of the data they store, such as uniqueness or ordering. To employ them, developers must either possess domain knowledge or transform their data to exhibit the desired property, which is a tedious, manual process. One such transformation---commonly used in data mining and program analysis---is data enumeration, where data items are assigned unique identifiers to enable fast equality checks and compact memory layout. In this paper, we present an automated approach to data enumeration, eliminating the need for manual developer effort. Our implementation in the MEMOIR compiler achieves speedups of 2.16x on average (up to 8.72x) and reduces peak memory consumption by 5.6% on average (up to 50.7%). This work shows that automated techniques can manufacture data properties to unlock specialized collection implementations, pushing the envelope of collection-oriented optimization.

Artifact Description:

Our artifact includes source files for the MEMOIR compiler, with the transformation and extensions described in the paper. In addition to this, it includes the benchmark suite used for evaluation, and plotting scripts. This artifact reports its results by recreating Figures 4, 5, 6, 8a and 9a of the paper. The user is able to configure which experiments they would like to evaluate, this customization is detailed in the artifact appendix. The artifact has been tested on both Intel-x64, AMD-x64, and AArch64. The artifact requires a network connection to download external dependencies and our benchmark suite.

metadata.title: HoneySat: A Network-based Satellite Honeypot Framework
metadata.description:
HoneySat: A Network-based Satellite Honeypot Framework
NDSS 2026 Artifact Evaluation - README

This artifact accompanies the NDSS 2026 paper:
HoneySat: A Network-based Satellite Honeypot Framework

The artifact provides a Dockerized version of HoneySat and evaluation scripts to reproduce the experiments in the paper.

  1. ARTIFACT CONTENTS AND GOALS

What this artifact provides:

  • Dockerized HoneySat deployments for:

    • CSP-based satellite missions

    • CCSDS/YAMCS-based satellite missions

  • Evaluation utilities demonstrating:

    • Believable telemetry and telecommand handling

    • Realistic communication windows

    • Interaction capabilities

    • Logging functionality

    • Configurability and extensibility

Paper claims supported:

Claim C1: HoneySat deceives adversaries and logs activity.

  • E1.1: Believable telemetry

  • E1.2: Realistic communication windows

  • E1.3: Interactive capabilities

  • E1.4: Logging of interactions

Claim C2: HoneySat supports multiple satellite protocol ecosystems.

  • E2: Configurable CSP and CCSDS/YAMCS deployments

  1. GETTING THE ARTIFACT

Artifact DOI:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17548980

Extract the artifact:

 
tar xzpvf ndss-artifact-eval.tar.gz cd ndss-artifact-eval

  1. SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS

Hardware:

  • ~25 GB free disk space

  • 4 CPU cores

  • 8 GB RAM

Software:

  • Linux system (verified on Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS)

  • Docker with Docker Compose
    Install instructions: https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/

  • Python 3.12 or newer

  • Python virtual environment (venv)

  • Bash

  • Telnet client

  • Modern web browser

Privileges needed:

  • Ability to bind local ports (80, 24, etc.)

  • Ability to run Docker

  1. REPOSITORY LAYOUT

deployment/
Dockerized HoneySat services and configuration.

evaluation/
Python utilities and experiment scripts.
Python dependencies in evaluation/requirements.txt.

  1. ENVIRONMENT SETUP

Create virtual environment:

 
python3 -m venv . source bin/activate

Install Python dependencies:

 
python3 -m pip install -r evaluation/requirements.txt

(Optional) Configure Docker user:

 
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER sudo reboot now

Verify:

 
docker ps

Start services (recommended: use convenience scripts):

 
./evaluation/experiment-1/run-experiment-csp.sh ./evaluation/experiment-1/run-experiment-ccsds.sh

  1. QUICK START FOR PASS SIMULATIONS

HoneySat simulates realistic satellite communication windows.

Two helper scripts start HoneySat and schedule an imminent pass.

CSP-based honeypot:

 
./evaluation/experiment-1/run-experiment-csp.sh

CCSDS/YAMCS-based honeypot:

 
./evaluation/experiment-1/run-experiment-ccsds.sh

  1. EXPERIMENT GUIDE

Assumptions:

  • Environment setup complete

  • Docker running

  • Commands executed from repository root

7.1. Experiment E1.1 - Believable Telemetry

Run:

 
./evaluation/experiment-1/run-experiment-ccsds.sh

Expected telemetry:

  • Voltage: ~8000 mV

  • Temperature: ~30 C

  • Current: ~74 mA

Supports claim C1.

7.2. Experiment E1.2 - Realistic Passes

Start:

 
./evaluation/experiment-1/run-experiment-csp.sh

Web interface:
http://localhost:80
Username: admin
Password: admin

Telnet interface:

 
telnet localhost 24 activate

Probe:

 
1: com_ping 10

Expected:

  • Responses only during predicted pass

  • Correct addressing: source 1, destination 10

Supports claim C1.

7.3. Experiment E1.3 - Interactive Capabilities

Once satellite is reachable:

 
1: obc_system [shell command]

Supports claim C1.

7.4. Experiment E1.4 - Logging Capabilities

Run:

 
python3 ./evaluation/experiment-1/python_dump_mongodb/dump_mongodb.py

Expected output:

  • Telecommands

  • Telemetry

  • Interaction metadata

  • Timestamps

Supports claim C1.

7.5. Experiment E2 - Customization and Extensibility

Navigate:

 
cd evaluation/experiment-2

Create configuration:

 
python3 ./honeysat.py [csp|ccsds] "SAT_NAME" "LOCATION"

Example:

 
python3 ./honeysat.py csp "BEESAT" "Berlin"

Start services:

 
python3 ./honeysat.py start [csp|ccsds] "SAT_NAME" "LOCATION"

Stop services:

 
python3 ./honeysat.py stop [csp|ccsds]

Supports claim C2.

metadata.title: Artifact for "TPDE: A Fast Adaptable Compiler Back-End Framework"
metadata.description:
Artifact for CGO 2026 paper "TPDE: A Fast Adaptable Compiler Back-End Framework"

Quick Start

Download the artifact.tar.gz, unpack it and download `tpde-cgo-bench-{aarch64,x86_64}.tar.gz` (depending on your CPU architecture) into the images subdirectory.

With SPEC

- Disable ASLR (`sudo echo 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space`, only needed for Copy-and-Patch benchmarks on x86-64) and SELinux (`sudo setenforce 0`)
- Mount/unpack the SPEC installer to some folder (for mounting use `sudo mount -o loop,ro,context="system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0" cpu2017-1.1.0.iso /mnt/cpu2017`)
- Run `SPEC_INSTALL_DIR=/mnt/cpu2017 DOCKER_TOOL=<docker/podman> make all-spec`
- Wait approximately 2 days
- There should now be a new folder called `latex.<long-name>` which contains a `figures_spec_<x86_64/aarch64>.pdf` with the main plots from the paper

Without SPEC

- Disable SELinux (`sudo setenforce 0`)
- Run `DOCKER_TOOL=<docker/podman> make all`
- Wait a few hours
- There should now be a new folder called `latex.<long-name>` which contains a `figures_<x86_64/aarch64>.pdf` with the main plots from the paper with the LLVM test-suite benchmarks substituded for the SPEC benchmarks

 

Note: The Umbra benchmark may be a bit unstable due to IO behavior and therefore the run-times (especially of TPDE-LLVM) may be larger than expected. If that happens you can repeat the Umbra benchmark using `make repeat-umbra` and then check the `figures_<x86_64/aarch64>.pdf` (not the SPEC version).

 

Artifact contents

The artifact contains two main components:
  - The main Makefile and all the files necessary to build the benchmarking containers
  - Prebuilt images for x86-64 and AArch64 in a benchmark and uber version.
  The benchmark images contain only the files necessary to run the benchmarks while the uber images contain all the build files as well
  to allow editing of the source code and running custom benchmarks.

The benchmarks include the following benchmarks:
  - SPEC CPU 2017 (only if you have the installation image available)
  - The LLVM test-suite as a freely available replacement for the SPEC benchmarks
  - The Umbra DBMS
  - Wasmtime sightglass benchmarks + PolyBench for WASM benchmarks (only x86-64)

Details are in the artifacts README.

metadata.title: SHLF - TIAM Tool: Technology–Innovation–Adoption–Market Analysis Workbook
metadata.description:
TIAM Analytics Tool: A Framework for Technology Impact Assessment & Comparative Benchmarking

Description

The SHLF TIAM Tool is a methodological artifact designed to operationalize the TIAM Method (Technology–Innovation–Adoption–Market) within the Systemic Hybrid Learning Framework (SHLF). It serves as a bridge between qualitative case study research and quantitative analysis, enabling the rigorous documentation of digital innovation processes.

By transforming unstructured company testimonies into semi-quantitative metrics, the tool empowers researchers to map technological initiatives against global IT macro-trends, assess their value creation potential, and evaluate cross-sector transferability.

Methodological Contribution

Unlike static data collection forms, this tool is engineered to ensure analytical and methodological consistency across multiple case studies. It standardizes the evaluation criteria, making qualitative data comparable and reproducible. This allows for valid cross-case analysis and the identification of systemic patterns in digital adoption.

Core Analysis Module (deep company analysis)

The framework utilizes standardized "Company Sheets" (e.g., Company_Kinetix) as structured analysis process. These modules perform four key analytical functions:

  1. Innovation Taxonomy: classifies initiatives by scope (Incremental vs. Radical) and type (Product vs. Process) to define the innovation's identity.
  2. Strategic Alignment: maps local initiatives against global IT Macro-Trends (e.g., AI, IoT, Cloud) and Industry 4.0 paradigms.
  3. Value Creation Logic: applies a weighted scoring model to quantify impacts on Efficiency, Customer Engagement, and ESG/Sustainability goals.
  4. Transferability Assessment: estimates the potential for expertise transfer to other industrial sectors (Cross-fertilization).

Synthesis Engine: The Comparative Matrix

The "3_Summary & Comparison" module acts as the synthesis engine of the workbook. It automatically aggregates data from individual cases to generate a Comparative Dashboard. This feature enables:

  • Benchmarking: Side-by-side visualization of Innovation Scores across different organizations.
  • Pattern Recognition: identification of correlations between specific technology adoption strategies and business performance.
  • Gap Analysis: visualizing the distance between a company's current maturity and market leaders.

Dual-Version Availability & Functionality 

To ensure maximum accessibility while offering advanced automation, the repository provides two distinct editions:

  1. Automated Edition (.xlsm - The Full Application) This version features a VBA-driven engine that automates the entire lifecycle of the analysis. By using the main control panel (Index), the tool performs the following actions automatically:
    • Sheet Generation: Instantly creates a new, dedicated worksheet for each new company based on the master template.
    • Navigation Structure: Automatically creates bi-directional navigation links between the Index and the specific company sheet.
    • Individual Visualization: Generates specific analysis charts (Radar & Bar charts) within the new company sheet.
    • Dynamic Benchmarking: Automatically injects the new company data into the "Summary & Comparison" module.
    • Global Updates: Refreshes all comparative charts (Scatter plots, Matrices) and updates graph legends to include the new entry without any manual range adjustment.
  2. Standard Edition (.xlsx - The Manual Template) A macro-free version designed for restrictive IT environments. It retains the full scoring logic but requires a manual workflow:
    • Users must manually duplicate the template sheet for new cases.
    • Data ranges in the summary charts must be updated manually to include new companies.
    • Ideal for archival purposes or strict security contexts.

Note

The tool is distributed with a pre-populated fictitious dataset (e.g., Puntofermo, Fucina) to demonstrate the visualization logic. Users are expected to input their own empirical data.

Target Audience

Designed for academic researchers, graduate students, and business analysts applying the SHLF methodology to conduct standardized evaluations of digital transformation.

metadata.title: mmcipher-artifact
metadata.description:
This is an artifact for: Hongxiao Wang, Ron Steinfeld, Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, Muhammed F. Esgin, and Siu-Ming Yiu: "mmCipher: Batching Post-Quantum Public Key Encryption Made Bandwidth-Optimal." To appear in USENIX Security 2026. Preprint: IACR ePrint 2025/1000

A multi-message multi-recipient PKE/KEM enables the batch encryption of multiple messages (as a message vector) for multiple independent recipients in a single operation, significantly reducing costs, particularly bandwidth, compared to the trivial solution of encrypting each message individually.

We provide self-contained Python and portable C implementations of the scheme (with some aspects that may need further optimization for production-level deployment). The artifact also contains the code used for generating the comparative benchmarks reported in this work, source code for ZK proof experiments using the LaZer Library, and scripts and tools used for security parameter selection (computation of lattice parameter sets and decryption failure probabilities).

metadata.title: Cultural Isomorphism in Financial Education: A Gamified Stochastic Model of Savings Horizons based on the 'Lucha Libre' Metaphor
metadata.description:
This software artifact (available for universal access at: (https://divulgandolasfinanzas-afk.github.io/Divulgando-las-Finanzas-Games/) presents a gamified behavioral intervention and stochastic model designed to strengthen long-term savings habits among the Mexican population. Grounded in the "Inclusión Financiera en México 2025" diagnostic, the project addresses the persistent gap between financial access (63% hold formal accounts) and effective usage, while combating the "lack of financial consciousness" and the cultural irrelevance of traditional educational materials.

The core methodology employs a Cultural Isomorphism strategy, utilizing the iconography of Mexican Lucha Libre . This approach reduces cognitive load for vulnerable populations by linking the abstract concept of saving to a culturally recognized combat system. The simulation models the savings lifecycle through a stochastic combat system where "good" and "bad" maneuvers simulate financial shocks (income variability vs. unexpected expenses), compelling real-time resource allocation decisions.

Users advance through three distinct arenas representing temporal savings horizons (Short-Term/Liquidity, Medium-Term/Security, and Long-Term/Capital Accumulation). The system employs adaptive feedback loops and aims to mitigate hyperbolic discounting biases and foster long-term planning resilience. This simulation protocol directly contributes to national strategic axes focused on social inclusion, poverty, and inequality.

metadata.title: Compilation of Generalized Matrix Chains with Symbolic Sizes
metadata.description:
Generalized Matrix Chains (GMCs) are products of matrices where each matrix carries features (e.g., general, symmetric, triangular, positive-definite) and is optionally transposed and/or inverted. GMCs are commonly evaluated via sequences of calls to BLAS and LAPACK kernels. When matrix sizes are known, one can craft a sequence of kernel calls to evaluate a GMC that minimizes some cost, e.g., the number of floating-point operations (FLOPs). Even in these circumstances, high-level languages and libraries, upon which users usually rely, typically perform a suboptimal mapping of the input GMC onto a sequence of kernels. In this work, we go one step beyond and consider matrix sizes to be symbolic (unknown); this changes the nature of the problem since no single sequence of kernel calls is optimal for all possible combinations of matrix sizes. We design and evaluate a code generator for GMCs with symbolic sizes that relies on multi-versioning. At compile-time, when the GMC is known but the sizes are not, code is generated for a few carefully selected sequences of kernel calls. At run-time, when sizes become known, the best generated variant for the matrix sizes at hand is selected and executed. The code generator uses new theoretical results that guarantee that the cost is within a constant factor from optimal for all matrix sizes and an empirical tuning component that further tightens the gap to optimality in practice. In experiments, we found that the increase above optimal in both FLOPs and execution time of the generated code was less than 15% for 95% of the tested chains.

 

This artifact contains the code generator for generalized matrix chains and the infrastracture to replicate the results in the associated paper.
